## Why This Is Asked

This question tests understanding of safe, per-tenant traffic experimentation without impacting production. It covers config-driven behavior, sidecar responsibilities, and end‑to‑end validation in a CNF gateway on Kubernetes.

## Key Concepts

- Traffic shadowing (mirroring) to a test shadow target
- Per-tenant configuration via Namespace ConfigMaps
- Fire-and-forget asynchronous forwards
- Deriving shadow path from tenant identity (X-TENANT-ID) and request path
- Observability: simple verification endpoint and metrics

## Code Example

```yaml
# Namespace ConfigMap (per-tenant) - cnf-shadow.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: cnf-shadow
  namespace: tenant-a
data:
  cnf.shadow.enabled: "true"
  cnf.shadow.percent: "10"
  cnf.shadow.target: "shadow-svc.tenant-a.svc.cluster.local"
```

```yaml
# Minimal Deployment patch to mount config via envFrom (sidecar example)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: cnf-gateway
  namespace: tenant-a
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: gateway
        image: your/gateway:latest
      - name: sidecar-shadow
        image: your/cnf-shadow-sidecar:latest
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: cnf-shadow
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you ensure idempotent shadow requests if the shadow target replays on failure?
- What metrics would you collect to validate shadow traffic distribution and detect drift from intended percent?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question evaluates candidate understanding of tenant-scoped dynamic capability negotiation and caching in cloud-native environments, ensuring isolation and correctness at scale.

## Key Concepts

- Tenant-scoped capability registry (implemented as a CRD or ConfigMap)
- Per-tenant, TTL-based cache in the sidecar for performance optimization
- Highest common version selection using semantic versioning
- HTTP 406 Not Acceptable response when no compatible version exists; graceful default fallback
- Observability: Prometheus metrics, structured logging, and distributed tracing

## Code Example

```go
// Pseudocode for version negotiation
func negotiate(upstreamVersions []string, tenantID string) string {
    tenantVersions := registry.GetVersions(tenantID)
    allowed := intersect(upstreamVersions, tenantVersions)
    if len(allowed) == 0 {
        return DEFAULT_VERSION
    }
    return highestVersion(allowed)
}
```

## Implementation Highlights

- Extract X-TENANT-ID header in sidecar middleware
- Query central registry for tenant capabilities
- Compute intersection with upstream supported versions
- Select highest compatible version using semver comparison
- Store result in tenant-scoped cache with configurable TTL
- Return 406 if negotiation fails and no default is configured
- Emit histogram metrics for negotiation latency and cache hit rates

## Why This Question Matters
This question evaluates practical, day-2 operational skills for implementing per-tenant rate limiting in CNF gateways—a common requirement in multi-tenant Kubernetes environments.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace-scoped configuration for feature toggles
- Sidecar pattern for tenant isolation
- Redis-based rate limiting with sliding window TTL and 429 responses

## Code Example
```go
func allow(tenant, path string) bool {
  key := tenant + ":" + pathHash(path)
  count, _ := redis.Incr(key).Result()
  if count == 1 { redis.Expire(key, time.Minute) }
  return count <= 100
}
```

## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates practical knowledge of cross-tenant isolation using runtime attestation (SPIRE) and policy enforcement (OPA) in CNF meshes. It assesses understanding of real-world challenges including tenant scoping, short-lived credential management, and gateway security enforcement.

## Key Concepts

- Service mesh RBAC, namespaces, and tenant-scoped ServiceAccounts
- End-to-end testing within a single namespace

apiVersion: spire.spiffe.io/v1alpha1
kind: ClusterSPIFFEID
metadata:
  name: cnf-workload
spec:
  spiffeIDTemplate: "spiffe://example.com/ns/{namespace}/tenant/{tenant_id}"
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:

  tenantIDLabel: "tenant.id"

# OPA Authorization Policy

kind: AuthorizationPolicy

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests practical disaster recovery design for CNF gateways with multi-tenancy, moving beyond high-level theory to real implementation.

## Key Concepts
- Kubernetes CRD design for per-tenant failover policies
- Control-plane health probes with configurable thresholds
- Traffic re-routing via Ingress/VirtualService resources
- TLS identity preservation using SPIFFE/SPIRE

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: cnf.example/v1
kind: TenantFailoverPolicy
metadata:
  name: tenant-a-failover
spec:
  tenant: tenant-a
  primaryGateway: gateway-a.tenant-a.svc
  standbyGateway: gateway-a-standby.tenant-a.svc
  unhealthyThreshold: 3
  failoverDelaySeconds: 5
  tlsIdentityRef:
    spireEntry: spiffe://cluster/tenant-a/gateway
```

```go
// Controller reconciliation logic (simplified)
func (r *TenantFailoverPolicyReconciler) Reconcile(ctx context.Context, req ctrl.Request) error {
    policy := &cnfv1.TenantFailoverPolicy{}
    if err := r.Get(ctx, req.NamespacedName, policy); err != nil {
        return err
    }

    // Poll control-plane health
    healthy := r.checkControlPlaneHealth(policy.Spec.Tenant)

    if !healthy {
        policy.Status.FailureCount++
        if policy.Status.FailureCount >= policy.Spec.UnhealthyThreshold {
            return r.executeFailover(policy)
        }
    } else {
        policy.Status.FailureCount = 0
    }
    return nil
}

func (r *TenantFailoverPolicyReconciler) executeFailover(policy *cnfv1.TenantFailoverPolicy) error {
    // Update Ingress to point to standby
    ingress := &networkingv1.Ingress{}
    r.Get(ctx, types.NamespacedName{Name: "gateway-ingress", Namespace: policy.Spec.Tenant}, ingress)
    ingress.Spec.Default.Backend.Service.Name = policy.Spec.StandbyGateway
    r.Update(ctx, ingress)

    // Update SPIRE TLS identity binding
    return r.updateSPIREEntry(policy)
}
```
